Yad Malachi Digitization — Pipeline Case Study

Verified Against the Ink

Every correction in this pipeline traces back to a real disagreement, resolved by looking at the actual 1851 page — not inferred, not guessed, and never applied without a human ruling. Here is what that looks like, word by word.

Method

How we look at a page

The same four-level zoom runs for every one of the 1,061 flagged word positions in klalim 1–222: a physical page, a line, a bounding box, and finally a structured record. Nothing here is inferred from a clean digital source — there isn't one. It starts as ink on paper.

LEVEL 1

The physical page

Page 40 of the Berlin (1851/2) scan, rendered directly from the source PDF. This is all any OCR engine has to work with — a single dense column running the full page width, a running header repeating the work's name, and a printer's letterforms nearly 175 years old. Four words on this one page are set with the wrong piece of type.

LEVEL 2

The line

Near the foot of that page, one line reads וכלבד where the sentence needs ובלבד ("provided that"). Document AI reads it exactly as printed; the stored text has the word the sentence requires. The two disagree — and that disagreement is what puts this word in front of a human.

LEVEL 3

The word, and its box

Every token Document AI extracts carries a bounding box — four numbers, normalized to a 0–1 fraction of the page's width and height, independent of resolution or DPI. That is what lets the pipeline re-crop this exact spot at 900 dpi, years after the original OCR pass ran, and hand a human only the pixels in question.

klal 88 · page 40 · 900 dpi
bbox  x1: 0.7742  y1: 0.8471  x2: 0.8199  y2: 0.8653
LEVEL 4

The structured record

Each flagged token becomes one JSON record: which klal, which page, what the two candidate readings were, the box to re-crop, and — once adjudicated — the model's verdict and confidence.

{
  "klal_id": 88,
  "page": 40,
  "opcode": "replace",
  "original_word": "וכלבד",
  "corrected_word": "ובלבד",
  "bbox": {
    "x1": 0.7742, "y1": 0.8471,
    "x2": 0.8199, "y2": 0.8653
  },
  "vision_selected": "B",
  "vision_confidence": 1.00
}

real record, corrections_verified_part1.json — option A is what the page literally shows, option B what the sentence requires; the vision pass chose B at full confidence, and a human still had to agree before it became text

Which raises the question the next section exists to answer: why does the printed page say וכלבד at all?

Not a misprint — a substitution

The compositor reached into the wrong box

Hebrew כ (kaf) and ב (bet) differ by one stroke: bet's base projects to the right, kaf's does not. This word needs a bet twice, and got one.

klal 88, page 40, at 900 dpi. Right to left: ו · כ · ל · ב · ד. The second letter has no base stroke. The fourth has one — a bet, in the same word, on the same line, out of the same forme.

That fourth letter is what makes this example worth having. A misreading would have to explain why the two shapes differ where the type set one letter; a poor scan would have to explain why the difference stays crisp at 900 dpi. What the page shows is a kaf-shaped sort in one position and a bet-shaped sort in the other, in a word that takes bet in both.

And not once. Four words on this single page are set with a kaf where the sentence requires a bet:

page 40, top to bottom — אכל for אבל · וכתכו for וכתבו · כתיכ for כתיב · וכלבד for ובלבד

וכתכו is the plainest of the four: the word wants kaf then bet, and the page shows the same sort twice. Four substitutions on one forme, all in the same direction, is not four slips of the hand — it is what a compositor's case running short of bet looks like.

Which matters well beyond the curiosity. An OCR engine returning וכלבד here is not wrong — that is what is printed. Any pipeline that scores its engines against a corrected text will book those four as recognition failures and learn the wrong lesson from them. They are not recognition failures. They are the 1851 compositor, faithfully recorded — and deciding what belongs in a digital edition, the ink as set or the word as meant, is an editorial judgement that belongs to a person, not to a confidence score.

The hard case

A boundary, not just a word

A wrong klal boundary is a different kind of defect from a wrong letter: the words are all present and correctly read, but attached to the wrong klal, so a citation resolves to the wrong place. This is the clearest example on file — klal 82's own closing citation ended up inside klal 83, and no purely semantic read caught it until someone laid the stored text next to the printed page and the raw extraction log.

Here is klal 83's own stored record, exactly as it sat before anyone touched it — this is the actual pre-fix text, not a paraphrase:

פג בשל בשל [.] דף ס"א ב' וש"ות זקן אהרן סי' קפ"ג : תורה הלך אחר המחמיר ובשל סופרים ה הלך אחר המקיל...

the actual pre-fix record, part1.json (git history) — klal_id 83, title field was literally "בשל בשל"

The cause is visible in Document AI's own raw token dump for this exact spot on the page (docai_word_boxes/page_38.json) — every token it extracted, in the order it extracted them, each with its true vertical position on the page (smaller y = higher up):

extracted as token # text y‑position what it is
522ישרא0.7407klal 82's own text — stops here, mid-word
523–524פג בשו0.7772klal 83's gematria + opening word, read once
525בשל0.7676the same word, detected and read a second time
526–536דף ס"א ב' וש"ות זקן אהרן סי' קפ"ג :0.7608klal 82's real citation — physically above both rows before it, extracted after them
537+תורה הלך אחר המחמיר ובשל סופרים...0.7720the rest of klal 83's real opening sentence

Two things are visible in this table at once. Klal 83 opens with a larger, decoratively set first letter — standard for a new klal in this print — and Document AI's layout analysis read that one physical word twice, as two separate tokens (בשו, then בשל). Both duplicates were extracted before the citation line, even though the citation's own y-position (0.7608) sits higher on the page — earlier in true reading order. Whatever stitches the running text together just walks the array in extraction order, so it reproduced both problems at once: a doubled opening word, then a citation that belongs to the klal above, then the real sentence. Untangled, it's one continuous line: בשל תורה הלך אחר המחמיר ובשל סופרים הלך אחר המקיל.

page 38 — klal 82's closing lines running directly into klal 83's opening, as actually printed

klal 82 — correct ending

דף ס״א ב׳ וש״ות זקן אהרן סי׳ קפ״ג

klal 83 — correct opening

פג בשל תורה הלך אחר המחמיר ובשל סופרים הלך אחר המקיל

Read together, the two klalim make a deliberate pair — biblical law leans strict, rabbinic law leans lenient, and klal 82 (בשל סופרים הלך אחר המקיל) is the counterpart klal 83 is built to answer. The scrambled version obscured that relationship entirely, and it's exactly the kind of error a text-only pass tends to miss: the broken version isn't ungrammatical, it's just wrong.

The hidden letter

One glyph, not two letters

The single most consequential defect in the corpus wasn't a misread letter or a misplaced sentence — it was a glyph this print uses that modern OCR has no concept of at all. Finding it took three independent kinds of evidence agreeing, not one confident-looking model output.

Klal 88, page 40. Document AI reads the word here as אא — aleph, aleph, twice in a row. That isn't a word. Here is the actual ink, at 1200dpi:

as OCR read it — "אא"

אא ← page 40, the disputed spot

an ordinary aleph, same line

תנא ← the alef here has no ascender

Look at the left character in the first crop: a tall hooked stroke rises well above the letter body — nothing like the plain aleph on the right, three words away on the same line. That ascender is a ל (lamed). This print sets אל as a single ligature glyph (Unicode U+FB4F); Document AI has no mapping for it, and reads the composite shape as a bare א, silently dropping the lamed. The word isn't אא — it's אלא, "but," one of the commonest words in the Talmudic vocabulary, its two letters fused by a 19th-century typesetter and split apart wrong by a 21st-century model that had never seen this sort before.

page 40, the full line — דשום תנא לא מחייב אלא א"כ הוציאו המצניע זולת רשב"א

One paleographic observation isn't proof by itself — an ascender could be ink bleed, a flaw in this one letterform, a coincidence. Two more signals, independent of the pixels and of each other, had to agree before this became a correction rather than a hunch:

Cross-engine. A second, independently-run OCR pass over this same page reads the identical glyph as a bare לא — keeping the lamed, dropping the aleph instead. Two engines splitting one composite shape in complementary directions is the signature of an unmapped ligature, not two unrelated mistakes.
confirmed
Semantics. Every reconstructed reading is the ordinary, contextually correct word — never a stretch. אינו אלא לא תעשה, קודם אלפא ביתא, בארץ ישראל — real Talmudic phrasing, not a word invented to make the sentence work.
confirmed
Negative control. Klal 44's א״א — a real abbreviation (אשת איש) — shows two plain alefs with a gershayim and no ascender on either. The discrimination is real; it isn't "ascenders everywhere."
confirmed

Once the mechanism was confirmed, it explained a pattern that had been sitting in the corpus for weeks under a different guise — a semantic spot-check had already flagged dozens of sentences that read as slightly-off gibberish, without knowing why. Every affected word turned out to be exactly a word where a ל immediately follows an א: אלא→אא, אליבא→איבא, אלעזר→אעזר, שמואל→שמוא, ישראל→ישרא — the mechanism's fingerprint, not eight unrelated coincidences.

{
  "decision_type": "manual_correction",
  "klal_id": 88,
  "word_index": 383,
  "candidate_snapshot": { "original_word": "אא" },
  "chosen_text": "אלא",
  "note": "Alef-lamed ligature correction ... Individually scan-verified against the ink at 600-1800 DPI."
}

real record, review_decisions.jsonl — one of 131 corrections across 51 klalim this mechanism produced, each recorded through the same flag → human-review → apply pipeline as every other correction in the corpus, never a direct edit.

Understanding the defect turned it from a hunt into a filter. A repair pass now restores the dropped ל automatically — arbitrated not by this project's own lexicon (which was built from this scan's OCR and had quietly absorbed the corruption) but by an independent 6.18-million-word reference corpus, where the collapsed form איבא occurs zero times and אליבא occurs 848.

Validated before it was trusted, against a reviewer's complete 22-decision pass over one klal: the raw engine reading agreed with the human 0 times out of 18; the repaired reading agreed 17 times out of 18, and made nothing worse.
0% → 94%
Checked against decisions already made. On 106 candidates the reviewer had already resolved by hand, the filter's verdict matched the human's in every single one.
106 / 106
A quarter of the review queue was this one worn sort. 118 of 538 candidates repair to exactly the stored text — meaning the disagreement never existed, and there was nothing for a human to adjudicate.
24% of the queue

Two rules held while building it. The raw engine reading is never overwritten — the repair is offered beside it, because a filter that rewrites history to look correct is not a fix. And items are flagged, not deleted: the test for flagging is an identity (repaired reading equals stored text), not a judgement call, which is the safest thing that can justify taking an item off a human's screen.

A substitution the pipeline found — and did not fix

The same substitution, in the other direction

The kaf-for-bet cluster is not an isolated habit of one forme. In the very first klal of the work (Klal 1, word 229) the compositor set a final Chet (ח) where the sentence needs a final Hei (ה), printing "דנראח" — and elsewhere in Part 1 the substitution runs the other way, a Hei standing in for a Chet. Measured across the reviewed third: 7 words printed with ח where ה belongs, and 5 with ה where ח belongs. Same shape as the bet shortage, same lesson. The corpus still reads דנראח today — emending a printed source is a human's ruling, not a detector's.

The detector evaluated the printed token against our 6.18-million-word Rabbinic corpus (Shulchan Arukh, Talmud Bavli, Mishneh Torah, Tur, Rashi) and flagged the anomaly:

Reading Word In Yad Malachi Corpus In Rabbinic Lexicon (S.A., T.B., etc.) Status
Printed (1851/2) דנראח 0 occurrences (unique misprint) 0 occurrences (makes no sense textually) Printer's error (ח/ה) — and still what the corpus stores
Proposed reading דנראה 3× in klalim 1–222 / 12× across all 667 43× across 6.18M words of core reference texts Flagged, awaiting a reviewer's ruling

The printed word "דנראח" (a) makes no sense in sentence context ("...דנראה מתוך דבריו..." — "as it appears from his words"), and (b) is nowhere else to be found: not once more in this work, and not once in a 6.18-million-word reference corpus spanning Shulchan Arukh, Talmud Bavli, Mishneh Torah, Tur and Rashi. The reading the sentence wants, "דנראה", is attested 43 times there and 12 times in this very book.

Which is exactly why it is flagged rather than fixed. An engine that silently "corrects" a 174-year-old printing is no longer transcribing it — and a reader who cannot tell an OCR artifact from an editorial emendation cannot trust either. The record shows the printed word, the proposed reading, and the evidence for it, and waits for a person to decide which belongs in the text. Twelve such letter substitutions are known in the reviewed third; every one of them is a decision waiting for a human, not a bug waiting for a patch.

Adjudication in the record

What the model actually sees

Three more disagreements from the automated pass — including a real-word substitution in the very first Klal — each resolved the same way: crop the exact box, show it to a vision model alongside both candidate readings, and require it to name which one the pixels actually support — never to invent a third option.

klal 21 · page 20confidence 0.98

Reads עורו, not עודו — resh, not dalet.

"Paleographically, the third letter features a smooth rounded shoulder characteristic of a resh, rather than a dalet. Contextually regarding Leviathan (Job 41), 'עורו קשה' ('his hide is tough') is the intended semantic meaning."

klal 218 · page 76confidence 1.00

Reads שגם, not שגס — final mem, not samech.

"Option B contains a typographical error with samech, which does not fit the letterform or the semantic context ('ושאפשר שגם רש״י סובר כן')."

klal 219 · page 76confidence 0.98

Reads האי, not האו — the standard Talmudic idiom.

"Contextually, 'האי תנא דבי ר' ישמעאל' ('this Tanna of the school of R. Ishmael') is a standard Aramaic Talmudic phrase, whereas 'האו' is a transcription error."

klal 1 · word 85 · page 14confidence 0.98

Reads לכו, not לכן — real-word substitution in the very first Klal. The crop above is the honest part: at 700 dpi that last letter still looks like a final nun. Both are real words, so no lexicon can separate them; only the sentence can.

"In context ('הואיל ויש משנה בידכם לכו אחריה'), the verb 'לכו' ('go / follow') is grammatically required. Both 'לכו' and 'לכן' are valid Rabbinic Hebrew words, and 19th-century final nun ('ן') and vav ('ו') differ by only 1–2 points in stroke length—meaning semantic reading comprehension is the only way forward."

Not every fix in the corpus comes from this automated pass. Klal 65's ב״ר→ב״ד correction, for instance, has no entry in the vision-adjudication cache at all — it was caught by direct human cross-reference against the scan and against Mishnah Eduyot 1:5, the ruling the klal actually states. The pipeline keeps that distinction on the record rather than blurring "verified by a person" into "verified by the model": the two are different kinds of evidence, and conflating them is exactly the failure mode the ledger below is trying to avoid.

Assembly

How structure becomes data

Once a klal's text is settled, it collapses into one record — the shape every one of Klalei HaGemara's 667 klalim takes on its way to becoming a Sefaria segment.

{
  "klal_id": 218,
  "gematria": "ריח",
  "section": "כללי ההא",
  "title": "הניחא למ\"ד מופנה מצד אחד למידין ואין משיבין וכו'",
  "clean_text": "ריח הניחא למ\"ד מופנה מצד אחד למידין... שגם רש\"י סובר כן...",
  "page": 76
}

real record, part1.json — one of 222 Part-1 klalim

And every batch of flagged candidates carries its own honesty check built in — a running list of which klalim the pipeline explicitly does not trust yet, so a downstream reviewer never mistakes silence for a clean bill of health:

{
  "total_candidates": 538,
  "klalim_covered": 157,
  "untrusted_klalim_excluded": []
}

The number nobody measures

Two engines agreeing is not proof

Every multi-engine OCR pipeline rests on one premise: different engines fail independently, so where they agree the reading is near-certain. It is the reason ensembles are trusted, and it is cheap to test. We tested it here.

26–41%chance the consensus reading is right when two distinct engines agree against the corpus — measured on this corpus
37cases of two or three engines producing the identical wrong reading, including unanimous 3-of-3
1worn printer's sort behind all of them — the ligature the section above dissects

The failure is not that the engines are weak. It is that architectural independence is defeated by a defect in the shared input: every reader is looking at the same ink, so a broken piece of type is upstream of all of them. Errors of that kind are not drawn at random from a vocabulary — they are drawn from what the glyph plausibly looks like, which is why three engines can be wrong the same way. A textbook-style independence estimate for this configuration puts such an agreement at roughly 3.5 × 10⁻⁷; here it happened 37 times in one pass.

Tightening the rule doesn't rescue it either. Requiring the primary engine to be one of the two, or demanding unanimity, was measured and rejected: three points of precision for 82% of the recall.

So agreement is used for what it is actually good for — deciding where a human should look first — and never for deciding what the text says. That is the difference between a pipeline that triages and one that quietly rewrites a book.

Where things actually stand

What's proven, and what isn't yet

The method holds up everywhere it has been run rigorously. It has not been run everywhere yet — and the difference matters more than the pitch.

Klalim 223–667 — text and page-level alignment are built; no witness set has been run there yet, and not one correction has been applied. That is a deliberate gate, not an oversight: a clean first third is not evidence the rest comes out clean by the same process.

Klalim with no extracted text at all — the chunker created the record and never filled it. All of them sit in klalim 223–667; the reviewed 1–222 have none. They export as an empty segment, never as their placeholder string, because fabricated text under a real citation address is the worst thing this pipeline could ship.

The case

287 dead citations become live links once, and stay that way.

Every example above is a real disagreement, resolved by looking at the actual page — the discipline the rest of the corpus still needs at scale. The harness is built and measured; what is left is a reviewer's time, and the two parts of the book it has not reached yet.
